claims.claim: 3D-SIM has inferior lateral (xy) resolution compared to STORM but offers flexibility in fluorophore selection and sample preparation for multi-color imaging.
claims.source: While the lateral (xy) resolution of 3D-SIM is inferior to that of STORM, the flexibility of fluorophore selection and sample preparation for multi-color imaging by 3D-SIM (Valli et al., 2021) allows us to easily locate target proteins relative to multiple centriolar markers.
claims.evidence: This is a technical comparison supported by citation to Valli et al., 2021.

claims.claim: FBF1 localizes between adjacent CEP164 structures in the axial view, identifying it as a distal appendage matrix protein.
claims.source: As an example, the localization of FBF1, which was positioned between adjacent CEP164 structures seen in the axial view of the published STORM picture (which the authors thus identified FBF1 as a distal appendage matrix protein) (Yang et al., 2018), was also recapitulated in our SIM image (see FBF1 top view in Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by both citation to Yang et al., 2018 and the authors' own SIM imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: CEP89 localizes near the subdistal appendage in addition to its distal appendage localization.
claims.source: We also observed localization of CEP89 near the subdistal appendage in addition to its distal appendage localization (CEP89 side view in Figure 1A), consistent with the previous report (Chong et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the authors' imaging data in Figure 1A and citations to Chong et al., 2020 and Yang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: CEP83 was shown to localize to the innermost position of the distal appendage when detected with an antibody recognizing the C-terminal region.
claims.source: CEP83 was shown to localize to the innermost position of the distal appendage (Bowler et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2018). We recapitulated this localization (see CEP83 inner ring in Figure 1A; Figure 1B) with the antibody used in the previous two papers (Bowler et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2018), which recognizes the C-terminal region of CEP83 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Bowler et al., 2019 and Yang et al., 2018, and the authors' own data in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The peak-to-peak diameter of the inner CEP83 ring is 308.6±4.9 nm.
claims.source: The peak-to-peak diameter of the inner CEP83 ring (308.6±4.9 nm, Figure 1C) was comparable to the previous report (313±20 nm) (Yang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a measurement from the authors' data shown in Figure 1C, compared to a cited value.

claims.claim: When detected with an antibody recognizing the middle part of CEP83, the protein localizes to a ring at the outermost part of the distal appendage with a diameter of 513.4±9.0 nm.
claims.source: However, when we detected this protein with the antibody that detects the middle part of the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), we observed the ring located at the outermost part of the distal appendage with the diameter of 513.4±9.0 nm (see CEP83 outer ring in Figure 1A; Figure 1B; Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a measurement from the authors' data shown in Figure 1A, 1B, and 1C.

claims.claim: Both CEP83 antibodies recognized a specific band at 80-110 kDa that is lost in CEP83 knockout cells.
claims.source: Both antibodies recognized the specific band at 80–110 kDa that is lost in the CEP83 knockout cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: CEP83 may have an extended configuration that spans 100 nm in length.
claims.source: One intriguing explanation for the difference in the ring diameter is that the protein might have an extended configuration that spans 100 nm (the difference in radius between inner and outer ring) in length.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the diameter measurements and structural predictions.

claims.claim: Human CEP83 protein is predicted to contain two conserved coiled-coil domains, one of which may span between 40-633 amino acids.
claims.source: Human CEP83 protein (Q9Y592) is predicted to contain two conserved coiled-coil domains, one of which may span between 40–633 amino acids.
claims.evidence: This is based on protein structure prediction.

claims.claim: The AlphaFold model of CEP83 shows a highly extended alpha-helical structure conserved among most species.
claims.source: Examination of the AlphaFold model (Jumper et al., 2021) of CEP83 shows a consistent highly extended alpha-helical structure, conserved among most species (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), supporting the model of CEP83 as a highly extended molecule.
claims.evidence: This is supported by AlphaFold structural predictions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and cited by Jumper et al., 2021.

claims.claim: One alpha helix contains 3.6 residues with a distance of 0.15 nm per amino acid.
claims.source: Since one alpha helix contains 3.6 residues with a distance of 0.15 nm per amino acid (Pauling et al., 1951) and contour length of an amino acid is around 0.4 nm (Ainavarapu et al., 2007), 400 amino acids stretch of coiled-coil domain as well as a disordered region that consists of 40 amino acids (the maximum distance between antigens of the two CEP83 antibodies) could contribute at least 76 nm.
claims.evidence: This is based on established structural parameters of alpha helices cited from Pauling et al., 1951 and Ainavarapu et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The contour length of an amino acid is around 0.4 nm.
claims.source: Since one alpha helix contains 3.6 residues with a distance of 0.15 nm per amino acid (Pauling et al., 1951) and contour length of an amino acid is around 0.4 nm (Ainavarapu et al., 2007), 400 amino acids stretch of coiled-coil domain as well as a disordered region that consists of 40 amino acids (the maximum distance between antigens of the two CEP83 antibodies) could contribute at least 76 nm.
claims.evidence: This is based on established structural parameters cited from Ainavarapu et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The length of immunoglobulin G (IgG) is approximately 8 nm.
claims.source: Since the length of immunoglobulin G (IgG) is ~8 nm (see Figure 2 of Tan et al., 2008), the primary and secondary antibodies at the two edges could contribute another ~30 nm.
claims.evidence: This is based on established antibody dimensions cited from Tan et al., 2008.

claims.claim: CEP83 forms an extended backbone scaffolding the distal appendage.
claims.source: This model, wherein CEP83 forms an extended backbone scaffolding the distal appendage, is attractive given that CEP83 is important for localization of all the other distal appendage proteins (Tanos et al., 2013) to different positions along the distal appendages (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their data and supported by citation to Tanos et al., 2013.

claims.claim: GFP fused to the C-terminus of CEP83 (CEP83-GFP) localized to a more inward and more basal centriolar position than CEP164 with a peak-to-peak diameter of 339.7±18.4 nm.
claims.source: Consistent with the endogenous CEP83 detected with the antibody that recognizes C-terminus of the protein, GFP fused to the C-terminus of CEP83 (CEP83-GFP) localized to more inward and more basal centriolar position than CEP164 with the peak-to-peak diameter of 339.7±18.4 nm, when the GFP was detected by antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-B.

claims.claim: GFP attached to the N-terminus of CEP83 (GFP-CEP83) was located at a similar position to CEP164 with a diameter of 425.5±17.5 nm.
claims.source: GFP attached to the N-terminus of CEP83 (GFP-CEP83) was located at the similar position to CEP164 with the diameter of 425.5±17.5 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C-D.

claims.claim: PIDD1 localizes to a ring with a similar diameter to CEP164 but is displaced distally in the side view.
claims.source: For the recently identified distal appendage protein, PIDD1 (Burigotto et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021), we observe a ring with a similar diameter to CEP164 but that was displaced distally in the side view (see PIDD1 in Figure 1A; Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1A and 1B, and supported by citations to Burigotto et al., 2021 and Evans et al., 2021.

claims.claim: PIDD1 localization is consistent with the localization of its functional partner ANKRD26.
claims.source: This localization is consistent with the localization of its functional partner ANKRD26 (Burigotto et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021; Figure 1A; Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1A and 1B, and supported by citations to Burigotto et al., 2021 and Evans et al., 2021.

claims.claim: KIZ localizes to a similar position as ANKRD26-PIDD1.
claims.source: KIZ (or Kizuna) was localized to the similar position to ANKRD26-PIDD1.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' localization studies.

claims.claim: LRRC45 is located at the innermost region of the distal appendage with the smallest ring diameter.
claims.source: LRRC45 was located at the innermost region of the distal appendage with the smallest ring diameter (Figure 1A; Figure 1B; Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1A, 1B, and 1C.

claims.claim: LRRC45 localization is similar to that of the inner ring of CEP83.
claims.source: This localization is similar to that of the inner ring of CEP83.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison based on the authors' localization data.

claims.claim: INPP5E was reported to localize to the distal appendage in cells grown with serum and redistribute to the cilium upon serum starvation.
claims.source: INPP5E was reported to localize to the distal appendage in the cells grown with serum and redistribute to the cilium once cells form the organelle upon serum starvation (Xu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2016.

claims.claim: INPP5E physically interacts with CEP164.
claims.source: This localization is also supported by the physical interaction between INPP5E and the distal appendage protein, CEP164 (Humbert et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Humbert et al., 2012.

claims.claim: INPP5E signal was observed around CEP164 in cells grown with serum, but a ninefold ring was rarely observed.
claims.source: Indeed, we observed the INPP5E signal around the distal appendage protein CEP164 in cells grown with serum, however, we rarely observed a ninefold ring (INPP5E in Figure 1A), typically observed with all other distal appendage proteins.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' imaging observations in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: INPP5E is not a stable component of distal appendages and instead transiently localizes around the distal appendage.
claims.source: Therefore, we were unable to measure the diameter of the ring formed by INPP5E. From this result, we think INPP5E is at least not a stable component of distal appendages and instead transiently localizes around the distal appendage.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the authors' imaging observations.

claims.claim: Localization of one set of distal appendage proteins (outer ring of CEP83, TTBK2, KIZ, PIDD1, and CEP89) was significantly enhanced following serum starvation.
claims.source: Localization of one set of the distal appendage proteins (outer ring of CEP83, TTBK2, KIZ, PIDD1, and CEP89) were significantly enhanced following the serum starvation, whereas another set of distal appendage proteins (FBF1, ANKRD26, CEP164, and LRRC45) were not affected (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Localization of another set of distal appendage proteins (FBF1, ANKRD26, CEP164, and LRRC45) was not affected by serum starvation.
claims.source: Localization of one set of the distal appendage proteins (outer ring of CEP83, TTBK2, KIZ, PIDD1, and CEP89) were significantly enhanced following the serum starvation, whereas another set of distal appendage proteins (FBF1, ANKRD26, CEP164, and LRRC45) were not affected (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: SCLT1 was the only distal appendage protein that decreased its centrosomal signal upon serum deprivation.
claims.source: SCLT1 was the only protein that decreased its centrosomal signal upon serum deprivation.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' quantitative analysis.

claims.claim: The centrosomal signal of all distal appendage proteins was barely or not detected in their respective knockout cells.
claims.source: In most cases, the centrosomal signal of distal appendage proteins were barely or not detected in their respective knockout cells (see for example Figure 2A, G, I), confirming that the antibodies detect specific proteins and that the semi-automated intensity measurement was working properly.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging and quantification data in Figure 2.

claims.claim: A weak signal of FBF1 was detected in FBF1 knockout cells despite the signal looking specific.
claims.source: Centriolar FBF1 signal looked specific as it is almost completely lost in CEP83 knockout cells, however, a weak signal of FBF1 was detected in FBF1 knockout cells (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Both FBF1 knockout clones had one nucleotide insertion between coding DNA 151 and 152 (151_152insT) in both alleles.
claims.source: Since both two FBF1 knockout clones had one nucleotide insertion in both alleles between coding DNA 151 and 152 (151_152insT) (Table 1B), which results in a premature stop codon at the codon 61, we assumed that the knockout cells express truncated protein via either alternative translation or alternative splicing.
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic DNA sequencing data presented in Table 1B.

claims.claim: The FBF1 knockout mutation results in a premature stop codon at codon 61.
claims.source: Since both two FBF1 knockout clones had one nucleotide insertion in both alleles between coding DNA 151 and 152 (151_152insT) (Table 1B), which results in a premature stop codon at the codon 61, we assumed that the knockout cells express truncated protein via either alternative translation or alternative splicing.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic sequence data.

claims.claim: CEP83 is the most upstream distal appendage protein.
claims.source: Consistent with the original study mapping new distal appendage proteins (Tanos et al., 2013), the centrosomal signal intensity of all the knockout cells were greatly diminished in CEP83 knockout cells (Figure 2A–K; Figure 2M), confirming that CEP83 is the most upstream.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by knockout analysis in Figure 2 and supported by citation to Tanos et al., 2013.

claims.claim: SCLT1 depletion showed substantial loss of localization of all other distal appendage proteins, including CEP83 and CEP89.
claims.source: SCLT1 depletion also showed substantial loss of localization of all the other distal appendage proteins, including CEP83 and CEP89 (Figure 2B–C; Figure 2F), suggesting that CEP83 and SCLT1 organize the distal appendage structure in a co-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by knockout analysis in Figure 2.

claims.claim: CEP83 and SCLT1 organize the distal appendage structure in a co-dependent manner.
claims.source: SCLT1 depletion also showed substantial loss of localization of all the other distal appendage proteins, including CEP83 and CEP89 (Figure 2B–C; Figure 2F), suggesting that CEP83 and SCLT1 organize the distal appendage structure in a co-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the knockout data in Figure 2.

claims.claim: SCLT1 knockout affected the localization of the outer ring of CEP83 much more strongly than the inner ring population.
claims.source: Note that the SCLT1 knockout affected the localization of the outer ring of CEP83 much more strongly than the inner ring population (Figure 2B; Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 2B and 2C.

claims.claim: The effect of SCLT1 knockouts was much stronger than previously reported using siRNA, likely because of complete absence of the protein in the knockout system.
claims.source: We observed a much stronger effect of SCLT1 knockouts than the previous report (Tanos et al., 2013), which used siRNA to deplete SCLT1, likely because of the complete absence of the protein in our knockout system.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between the authors' data and a cited study, with an interpretation of the difference.

claims.claim: TTBK2 localization at the distal appendage is largely dependent on CEP164.
claims.source: Consistent with the previous report (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014), TTBK2 localization at the distal appendage was largely dependent on CEP164, as the TTBK2 signal in CEP164 knockout cells was at an undetectable level similar to TTBK2 knockout cells (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by knockout analysis in Figure 2H and supported by citation to Čajánek and Nigg, 2014.

claims.claim: TTBK2 knockout affected localization of CEP164, the outer ring CEP83, FBF1, ANKRD26, PIDD1, and NCS1.
claims.source: Downstream of CEP164, TTBK2 knockout affected localization of CEP164, the outer ring CEP83, FBF1, ANKRD26, PIDD1, and NCS1 (Figure 2A; Figure 2C; Figure 2E; Figure 2G; Figure 2K; Figure 2M).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by knockout analysis in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The decrease of CEP164 intensity in TTBK2 knockout cells is consistent with CEP164 being a substrate of TTBK2.
claims.source: The decrease of CEP164 intensity in TTBK2 knockout cells is consistent with the observation that CEP164 is a substrate of TTBK2 and that centriolar CEP164 localization was markedly increased upon overexpression of wild type but not kinase-dead TTBK2 (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the authors' data and supported by citation to Čajánek and Nigg, 2014.

claims.claim: CEP83 is a substrate of TTBK2.
claims.source: Interestingly, localization of another TTBK2 substrate, CEP83 (Bernatik et al., 2020; Lo et al., 2019), was also affected by TTBK2 depletion (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Bernatik et al., 2020 and Lo et al., 2019, and demonstrated by data in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Only the outer ring of CEP83 was affected by TTBK2 knockout.
claims.source: Since only the outer ring of CEP83 was affected by TTBK2 knockout, we predict that CEP83 phosphorylation by TTBK2 induces a conformational change of CEP83 enabling the protein to organize the backbone of the distal appendage.
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' knockout data and is used to support a prediction.

claims.claim: CEP83 phosphorylation by TTBK2 may induce a conformational change enabling the protein to organize the backbone of the distal appendage.
claims.source: Since only the outer ring of CEP83 was affected by TTBK2 knockout, we predict that CEP83 phosphorylation by TTBK2 induces a conformational change of CEP83 enabling the protein to organize the backbone of the distal appendage.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the authors' data.

claims.claim: FBF1, ANKRD26, PIDD1, and NCS1 may be potential substrates of TTBK2, or their localization may be affected by phosphorylation of CEP83 or CEP164.
claims.source: The localization changes of FBF1, ANKRD26, PIDD1, and NCS1 also suggest that these proteins may be potential substrates of TTBK2, or the localization of these proteins may be affected by phosphorylation of CEP83 or CEP164.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the authors' observations of localization changes.

claims.claim: The effect of TTBK2 depletion emphasizes that CEP164-TTBK2 complex organizes a positive feedback loop for other distal appendage proteins to maintain structural integrity.
claims.source: In any case, the effect of TTBK2 depletion emphasizes that CEP164-TTBK2 complex (Čajánek and Nigg, 2014) organizes a positive feedback loop for other distal appendage proteins to maintain the structural integrity of the distal appendages (Figure 2N).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the authors' data and supported by citation to Čajánek and Nigg, 2014.

claims.claim: ANKRD26 depletion drastically affected its functional partner PIDD1.
claims.source: Interestingly, ANKRD26 depletion drastically affected not only its functional partner, PIDD1 (Burigotto et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021; Figure 2K), but also the outer ring of CEP83 (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by knockout analysis in Figure 2K and supported by citations to Burigotto et al., 2021 and Evans et al., 2021.

claims.claim: ANKRD26 depletion drastically affected the outer ring of CEP83.
claims.source: Interestingly, ANKRD26 depletion drastically affected not only its functional partner, PIDD1 (Burigotto et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021; Figure 2K), but also the outer ring of CEP83 (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by knockout analysis in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: ANKRD26 may be crucial for maintaining the protein structure of CEP83 at the outer part of the distal appendages.
claims.source: This might suggest that ANKRD26 may be crucial for maintaining the protein structure of CEP83 at the outer part of the distal appendages.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the knockout data.

claims.claim: The diminished CEP164 level in ANKRD26 knockout cells might be explained by its direct effect or an indirect effect through the outer ring of CEP83.
claims.source: The diminished CEP164 level in ANKRD26 knockout cells (Figure 2A; Figure 2M) might be explained by its direct effect or an indirect effect through the outer ring of CEP83.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the knockout data in Figure 2A and 2M.

claims.claim: LRRC45 knockout did not affect FBF1 localization, contrary to a previous publication.
claims.source: In contrast to a previous publication (Kurtulmus et al., 2018), we did not see the effect of LRRC45 on FBF1 localization (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is based on the authors' knockout data in Figure 2E and contrasts with a cited study.

claims.claim: The difference between the current study and Kurtulmus et al., 2018 regarding LRRC45's effect on FBF1 might come from differences in experimental setting (siRNA versus knockout).
claims.source: This difference might come from the difference in the experimental setting (e.g. siRNA versus knockout).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the source of discrepancy between studies.

claims.claim: The signal intensity of subdistal appendage marker CEP170 was not affected by any of the distal appendage proteins.
claims.source: The signal intensity of a marker of the subdistal appendage, CEP170, was not affected by any of the distal appendage proteins (Figure 2L) suggesting that distal appendage proteins are not required for the localization of subdistal appendage proteins at least in terms of signal intensity.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 2L.

claims.claim: Distal appendage proteins are not required for the localization of subdistal appendage proteins in terms of signal intensity.
claims.source: The signal intensity of a marker of the subdistal appendage, CEP170, was not affected by any of the distal appendage proteins (Figure 2L) suggesting that distal appendage proteins are not required for the localization of subdistal appendage proteins at least in terms of signal intensity.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data in Figure 2L.

claims.claim: The localization changes of distal appendage proteins were mostly not due to changes in expression level except that KIZ was highly destabilized in SCLT1 knockout cells.
claims.source: The localization changes were mostly not due to the changes in the expression level except that protein KIZ was highly destabilized in SCLT1 knockout cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Depletion of CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, or TTBK2 severely disrupted cilium formation in 24- or 48-hour serum-starved cells.
claims.source: The depletion of each component that is important for structural integrity of distal appendages (CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, TTBK2) severely disrupted the cilium formation in either 24- or 48 hr serum-starved cells (Figure 5A, B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliation assay data in Figure 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 modestly affected cilium formation at 24 hours after serum removal.
claims.source: FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 modestly affected cilium formation at 24 hr after serum removal (Figure 5A), but the ciliation defect in the knockout cells were ameliorated by prolonged incubation (48 hr) following serum starvation (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliation assay data in Figure 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: The ciliation defect in FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 knockout cells was ameliorated by prolonged incubation (48 hours) following serum starvation.
claims.source: FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 modestly affected cilium formation at 24 hr after serum removal (Figure 5A), but the ciliation defect in the knockout cells were ameliorated by prolonged incubation (48 hr) following serum starvation (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliation assay data in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 are important for cilium formation, but cells can compensate for their lack and slowly form primary cilia.
claims.source: This suggests that these proteins are important for cilium formation, but that cells can compensate for the lack of these proteins and slowly catch up to form primary cilia.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the ciliation assay data.

claims.claim: KIZ, LRRC45, and INPP5E had no effect on cilium formation.
claims.source: The distal appendage protein KIZ and LRRC45, as well as the distal appendage-associated protein, INPP5E, had no effect on cilium formation (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliation assay data in Figure 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: Ciliary length was mildly affected in FBF1 and INPP5E knockout cells at 24 hours.
claims.source: Ciliary length was mildly affected in FBF1 and INPP5E knockout cells at the earlier time point (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliary length measurements in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Shorter ciliary length was observed in ANKRD26 knockout cells serum starved for either 24 or 48 hours.
claims.source: Shorter ciliary length was observed in ANKRD26 knockout cells serum starved for either 24 or 48 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ciliary length measurements in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: ARL13B signal intensity inside the cilium was diminished in FBF1, CEP89, or ANKRD26 knockout cells even after 48 hours of serum starvation.
claims.source: Interestingly, ARL13B signal intensity inside the cilium was diminished in FBF1, CEP89, or ANKRD26 knockout cells even after the cells largely caught up on cilium formation after 48 hr of serum starvation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ARL13B intensity measurements in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 knockouts can slowly form cilia, but the slowly formed cilia may not be functionally normal.
claims.source: This suggests that these knockouts can slowly form cilia, but the slowly formed cilia may not be functionally normal.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the ARL13B intensity data.

claims.claim: The stronger defect in ciliary ARL13B signal in ANKRD26 might suggest a direct role of this protein in ARL13B recruitment around the distal appendages.
claims.source: The stronger defect in ciliary ARL13B signal in ANKRD26 might suggest a direct role of this protein in ARL13B recruitment around the distal appendages.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the ARL13B intensity data.

claims.claim: CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2 severely disrupted preciliary vesicle recruitment.
claims.source: Consistent with their critical role in the structural integrity of the distal appendages, CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2 severely disrupted preciliary vesicle recruitment (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by preciliary vesicle recruitment assay data in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: CEP89 modestly but significantly affected preciliary vesicle recruitment.
claims.source: Interestingly, CEP89 but not the other distal appendage proteins modestly but significantly affected preciliary vesicle recruitment (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by preciliary vesicle recruitment assay data in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The importance of CEP89 in preciliary vesicle recruitment is largely consistent with a previous report.
claims.source: The importance of CEP89 in preciliary vesicle recruitment is largely consistent with a previous report (Sillibourne et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with a cited study.

claims.claim: CP110 removal was severely affected in knockouts of CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2.
claims.source: CP110 removal was again severely affected in knockouts of the four integral components of the distal appendages (CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2) (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by CP110 removal assay data in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: CEP89 depletion partially inhibited CP110 removal.
claims.source: CEP89 depletion partially inhibited CP110 removal (Figure 5D), correlating with the partial effect on preciliary vesicle recruitment, which is upstream of CP110 removal (Figure 4L).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by CP110 removal assay data in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: IFT88 recruitment was severely disturbed in knockouts of CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2, but not in other knockouts.
claims.source: IFT88 recruitment was severely disturbed in the knockouts of the four integral components (CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2), but not in the other knockouts (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by IFT88 recruitment data in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The effect of CEP164 or TTBK2 on IFT88 recruitment was slightly stronger than CEP83 or SCLT1.
claims.source: The effect of CEP164 or TTBK2 was slightly stronger than CEP83 or SCLT1, suggesting that CEP164 and TTBK2 may be more directly involved in this process.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the IFT88 recruitment data.

claims.claim: CEP19 recruitment was strongly dependent on CEP164-TTBK2.
claims.source: CEP19 recruitment was strongly dependent on CEP164-TTBK2 (Figure 5F), but was only mildly affected by CEP83-SCLT1, which recruit CEP164 to the distal appendages (Figure 2A and N).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by CEP19 recruitment data in Figure 5F.

results.result: Distal appendages are ninefold symmetric blade-like structures attached to the distal end of the mother centriole, which is distinguished from the daughter centriole by possession of these structures along with subdistal appendages.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7, C10, C11, and C12 are well-established structural descriptions of centrioles and distal appendages supported by extensive prior literature citations. These represent foundational knowledge in the field rather than novel findings from this manuscript.

results.result: Distal appendages regulate four critical steps of cilium formation: preciliary vesicle recruitment, IFT protein complex recruitment, CEP19-RABL2 complex recruitment for IFT initiation, and CP110 removal from the mother centriole.
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C13-C18 summarize established functions of distal appendages supported by multiple prior studies. While the manuscript provides new experimental evidence for these functions, the basic framework was previously known. This represents important background rather than a primary novel finding.

results.result: Three new distal appendage proteins were identified: KIZ, NCS1, and CEP15 (previously named C3ORF14).
results.evaluation: Claim C23 represents a primary finding of the manuscript identifying three new distal appendage proteins. The identification is supported by localization data shown in Figure 1 and functional characterization throughout the manuscript. This expands the known repertoire of distal appendage components.

results.result: CEP83 forms an extended structure spanning from the innermost to outermost regions of the distal appendage, with the C-terminus localizing to an inner ring (diameter ~309 nm) and the middle region localizing to an outer ring (diameter ~513 nm), consistent with AlphaFold predictions of an extended alpha-helical structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C41 present a novel structural model for CEP83 supported by multiple lines of evidence: antibody epitope mapping (C29-C32), diameter measurements (C30-C31), GFP-tagging experiments (C40-C41), and AlphaFold structural predictions (C35). The calculations based on alpha helix geometry (C36-C38) provide theoretical support. This represents a significant advance in understanding distal appendage architecture.

results.result: Precise localization of distal appendage proteins was determined by 3D-SIM, showing FBF1 between adjacent CEP164 structures, CEP89 near both distal and subdistal appendages, PIDD1 and ANKRD26 at similar positions displaced distally, KIZ at a similar position to ANKRD26-PIDD1, and LRRC45 at the innermost region.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C46 present detailed localization data for multiple distal appendage proteins using 3D-SIM imaging (Figure 1A-B). The results are largely consistent with prior STORM studies (C27-C28) while adding new information about recently identified proteins (C42-C46). The data quality appears robust with clear imaging evidence.

results.result: INPP5E signal was observed around CEP164 in serum-fed cells but rarely formed a ninefold ring, suggesting INPP5E is not a stable component of distal appendages but instead transiently localizes around them.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 characterize INPP5E localization, distinguishing it from stable distal appendage components. The observation that INPP5E lacks the characteristic ninefold ring pattern (C49) supports the interpretation of transient localization (C50). This is consistent with prior reports of INPP5E redistribution upon serum starvation (C47).

results.result: Upon serum starvation, localization of outer ring CEP83, TTBK2, KIZ, PIDD1, and CEP89 was significantly enhanced, while FBF1, ANKRD26, CEP164, and LRRC45 were unaffected, and SCLT1 decreased.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 present quantitative data on how serum starvation affects distal appendage protein localization (Figure 1D). The differential responses suggest functional heterogeneity among distal appendage proteins. The data appear statistically robust with appropriate replication.

results.result: CRISPR-Cas9 knockout analysis revealed a more complex and interconnected hierarchy of distal appendage protein recruitment than previously described, with CEP83 as the most upstream protein and SCLT1 showing co-dependent organization with CEP83.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C58-C62 present a refined hierarchical model based on comprehensive CRISPR knockout analysis (Figure 2). The finding that SCLT1 affects CEP83 localization (C59-C60) revises the simple linear hierarchy, revealing bidirectional dependencies. The stronger effects compared to prior siRNA studies (C62) likely reflect complete protein absence in knockouts.

results.result: CEP164-TTBK2 forms a critical protein module that organizes a positive feedback loop to maintain distal appendage structural integrity, with TTBK2 phosphorylating CEP164 and CEP83 to stabilize their localization and potentially inducing conformational changes in CEP83.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C63-C70 characterize the CEP164-TTBK2 module's role in distal appendage organization. The data show TTBK2 depends on CEP164 for localization (C63) and affects multiple downstream proteins (C64). The phosphorylation relationships (C65-C66) are supported by prior literature. However, the proposed conformational change mechanism (C68) and substrate predictions (C69) are speculative and require further validation.

results.result: ANKRD26 depletion drastically affected its functional partner PIDD1 and the outer ring of CEP83, suggesting ANKRD26 may be crucial for maintaining CEP83 protein structure at the outer distal appendage region.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 demonstrate ANKRD26's role in distal appendage organization through knockout analysis (Figure 2). The effect on both PIDD1 (C71) and outer CEP83 (C72) is well-documented. However, the proposed mechanism for maintaining CEP83 structure (C73-C74) is speculative and requires additional structural or biochemical evidence.

results.result: LRRC45 knockout did not affect FBF1 localization (contrary to prior siRNA studies), and distal appendage protein knockouts did not affect subdistal appendage marker CEP170 intensity, with most localization changes not due to expression level changes except KIZ destabilization in SCLT1 knockouts.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C79 present negative results and controls that strengthen the overall study. The discrepancy with prior LRRC45 studies (C75-C76) highlights differences between siRNA and knockout approaches. The CEP170 data (C77-C78) demonstrate specificity of distal appendage protein functions. The immunoblot data (C79) confirm localization changes reflect recruitment rather than expression.

results.result: Depletion of CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, or TTBK2 severely disrupted cilium formation, while FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 showed modest defects at 24 hours that were ameliorated by 48 hours, and KIZ, LRRC45, and INPP5E had no effect on ciliation.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 present functional ciliation assays (Figure 5A-B) that distinguish critical structural components (CEP83-SCLT1-CEP164-TTBK2) from proteins with more subtle or compensable roles. The temporal analysis (C81-C83) reveals that some proteins affect ciliation kinetics rather than absolute capacity. The data are well-replicated with appropriate statistics.

results.result: Ciliary length was mildly affected in FBF1 and INPP5E knockouts at 24 hours, shorter in ANKRD26 knockouts at both timepoints, and ARL13B signal intensity was diminished in FBF1, CEP89, and ANKRD26 knockouts even after 48 hours, suggesting these proteins affect ciliary quality.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C89 provide additional functional characterization beyond simple ciliation frequency (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The ARL13B intensity data (C87-C88) suggest qualitative defects in cilia that form in certain knockouts. However, the speculation about ANKRD26's direct role in ARL13B recruitment (C89) requires further mechanistic investigation.

results.result: CEP89 selectively functions in RAB34+ preciliary vesicle recruitment, showing modest but significant effects, while CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2 severely disrupted vesicle recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C90-C92 identify CEP89's specific role in vesicle recruitment (Figure 5C). The selective function of CEP89 (C91) distinguishes it from structural components that affect all ciliogenesis steps. The consistency with prior reports (C92) strengthens confidence. This represents an important functional distinction among distal appendage proteins.

results.result: CP110 removal was severely affected in CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2 knockouts, and partially inhibited by CEP89 depletion, correlating with its effect on upstream vesicle recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 demonstrate CP110 removal defects in key distal appendage protein knockouts (Figure 5D). The partial effect of CEP89 (C94) is consistent with its role in vesicle recruitment, supporting a pathway relationship. The data quality appears robust with appropriate quantification.

results.result: IFT88 recruitment was severely disturbed in CEP83, SCLT1, CEP164, and TTBK2 knockouts (with CEP164/TTBK2 effects slightly stronger), while CEP19 recruitment was strongly dependent on CEP164-TTBK2 but only mildly affected by CEP83-SCLT1, suggesting CEP164-TTBK2 more directly regulates these processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C100 characterize IFT and CEP19 recruitment requirements (Figure 5E-F). The differential effects between CEP83-SCLT1 and CEP164-TTBK2 (C96-C100) suggest the latter module has more direct functional roles beyond structural organization. The interpretation that small amounts of CEP164-TTBK2 suffice for CEP19 recruitment (C99) is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: The CEP83-SCLT1 structural module recruits CEP164-TTBK2 to stabilize distal appendages, with CEP164-TTBK2 playing a more direct role in cilium formation by regulating preciliary vesicle recruitment, IFT/CEP19 recruitment, and CP110 removal, while CEP89 is dispensable for structural integrity but crucial for vesicle recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C101-C103 synthesize the functional data into a coherent model distinguishing structural from functional roles. The evidence from multiple assays (Figures 5 and 6) supports this hierarchical functional organization. This represents a major conceptual advance in understanding how distal appendages coordinate multiple ciliogenesis steps.

results.result: RAB34 localizes to centriole-associated vesicles and is important for preciliary vesicle recruitment/formation or fusion. RAB34 and MYO5A localization are highly coupled, with the highest percentage of double-positive centrioles in confluent serum-fed cells, representing the earliest vesicle markers to date.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C110 characterize RAB34 as a vesicle marker based on prior literature (C104-C106) and new colocalization data with MYO5A (C107-C108, Figure 3A-B). The temporal analysis (C108, C111) supports RAB34/MYO5A as early markers. However, the claim relies heavily on prior studies for RAB34's functional importance.

results.result: EHD1 and PACSIN2 are recruited to centrosomes later than MYO5A and RAB34 after serum withdrawal. RAB34 does not localize to the pericentriolar region (unlike MYO5A), making it a more suitable marker for assessing preciliary vesicle recruitment at distal appendages.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C114 establish RAB34 as superior to MYO5A for studying distal appendage vesicles based on temporal recruitment data (C111, Figure 3C-D) and spatial specificity (C113, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). This represents an important methodological advance for the field.

results.result: RAB34 localizes distal to and inward from CEP164, with MYO5A at the edge of RAB34 distribution on vesicles (separated by 67-89 nm). RAB34 vesicles measure approximately 190-230 nm × 170 nm × 190-250 nm, consistent with electron microscopy observations of vesicle-distal appendage positioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C123 provide detailed spatial characterization of RAB34 and MYO5A on vesicles using super-resolution microscopy (Figure 3H-K). The measurements (C120-C121) are precise and well-documented. The consistency with EM studies (C117) and mouse phenotypes (C115) strengthens confidence. This represents high-quality structural characterization.

results.result: RAB34 depletion significantly inhibited cilium formation and vesicle recruitment (only 1/18 RAB34-depleted mother centrioles had vesicles vs 16/41 controls at 3 hours), while MYO5A depletion did not affect ciliogenesis, consistent with RAB34's importance for initial vesicle recruitment/formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C129 demonstrate RAB34's functional importance through ciliation assays (Figure 4A) and electron microscopy (Figure 4B-C). The EM quantification (C128) provides strong evidence for vesicle recruitment defects. The lack of MYO5A effect (C126) is consistent with Griscelli syndrome phenotypes (C127). The statistical analysis appears appropriate (p<0.0054).

results.result: CP110 removal was modestly affected in RAB34 knockout cells, while IFT and CEP19 recruitment were not affected, suggesting preciliary vesicle recruitment is partially important for triggering CP110 removal.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C132 establish pathway relationships through functional assays (Figure 4D-F). The selective effect on CP110 removal (C130) without affecting IFT/CEP19 recruitment (C131) supports the interpretation of partial pathway dependence (C132). However, the authors note this differs from some prior studies, possibly due to timing differences.

results.result: IFT52 and FOP depletion greatly diminished IFT protein and CEP19 localization and inhibited ciliation, but did not disrupt preciliary vesicle recruitment, suggesting distal appendages independently regulate vesicle and IFT/CEP19 recruitment, while CP110 removal is partially downstream of vesicle recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C137 establish pathway independence through epistasis analysis (Figure 4G-K). The finding that IFT/CEP19 pathway disruption doesn't affect vesicle recruitment (C135-C136) demonstrates parallel pathways. The summary model (C137, Figure 4L) is well-supported by the data and represents an important conceptual advance.
